narrative.what_i_did:
This was a field-test-driven session — the operator was on their phone watching the wallet behave and surfaced four things in sequence, each of which I grounded against the actual code before acting rather than trusting the symptom description. It produced three commits, all of which landed on main at the operator's explicit instruction at the end, with all four gates green before the push.

The first two prompts were about the comms loop itself and turned out to need no code. The operator asked what happens to the stop hooks and writing to the next carpenter; I read .claude/hooks/session-close.sh and session-start.sh and explained the reinforcing loop honestly — the Stop/PreCompact hook archives and pushes session.json only when the carpenter has actually overwritten it, with a byte-comparison idempotency guard that no-ops otherwise, and on a dispatch branch it pushes via the branch:main refspec per PFOR-016. A Stop-hook git-check warning about untracked files turned out to be a transient sampling before the prior checkpoint settled — the tree was clean and the branch matched origin, nothing to do.

The third prompt — 'cloud not refreshing it's stale' — I first mis-scoped as the cockpit reading a stale session.json narrative (which was independently true — the narrative was five days and roughly thirty commits behind HEAD). The chip-form answer 'Cloud backup in app' corrected me: this was the in-app Supabase backup banner, and the operator clarified the banner was stuck. I traced walletStore, backupBanner, remoteStore, and WalletProvider and found the real bug: the red 'Cloud backup is failing' banner's Retry button was wired as onClick voiding save() — the void swallowed the promise rejection, so a continued remote failure gave zero on-screen feedback and the banner looked frozen. Commit c0d2ab3 added a retryState of idle, retrying, or failed: the button shows 'Retrying' and disables in flight, a repeated failure surfaces an inline re-sign-in nudge pointing at the real root cause (an expired Supabase session on a long-lived PWA), and a success silently clears via the existing prefs reload. It also covers the idle-lock case where save() throws before the push.

The fourth prompt was about the version-checker and refresh banner with comfortable tap padding. Grounding caught that this already shipped yesterday as commit 133790e — UpdateBanner.tsx with safe-area-inset-top plus 1rem padding, checkForUpdate.ts, useUpdateAvailable.ts, all wired in App. The chip-form answer was 'it's not firing — debug it.' I verified the whole detection chain is correct (version.json emitted, the version token substituted, a no-store plus nonce fetch, Netlify serving it fresh) and concluded the non-firing is bootstrap timing — the installed PWA predates the checker, and the banner can only announce a build newer than the running one. The operator chose 'just the SW cleanup,' so commit 8bb6873 added a network-only bypass for /version.json in public/sw.js, fixing a real leak where the nonce'd probe was caching one dead shell-cache entry per check.

The fifth prompt asked where the Nostr settings are and whether to add an old pubkey to the profile or take it as a new key. I read SettingsScreen, nostrProfile, the import flow, and RotateKeySection, then corrected the premise honestly: a public key can never become a signing key (cryptographically impossible), and a Nostr profile carries no pubkey field. The chip-form clarified the operator has the old nsec and wants this wallet to BECOME that identity while keeping its holdings. I then dug into the chassis (wallet.ts snapshot and fromSnapshot, succession.ts createSuccessionLink) and found the clean non-destructive path: rotate-to-supplied-key. Commit 38e8409 shipped adoptExistingKey.ts — the current active key signs a succession link binding current to old, the wallet rebuilds with the old key active and the current key retired, identity unchanged, holdings preserved (they verify because the chain walks back from the genesis they were signed under), and future Nostr events publish under the old npub. Persistence routes through saveWallet so the v2 K_data is REUSED — a fresh K_data would have silently invalidated distributed recovery-cohort shares, which I caught and fixed mid-build. Ten tests. AdoptExistingKeySection.tsx is the Settings UI under Rotate, behind a hard acknowledgement panel. Adding the adoptKey context callback pushed WalletProvider two lines over the 800-line hard limit, so I extracted the three transport-publish callbacks into useTransportPublish.ts (behavior-identical) rather than shaving comments — net the provider dropped to 773. Bundle budgets bumped for WalletProvider and SettingsScreen with audit comments.

The sixth prompt — 'messages still work?' — I answered with a pure verification pass and no code: chat and inbox both subscribe across recipient.keyHistory and decrypt via nip44DecryptFromAnyKey, and the transport effect keys on activeKey so it re-opens on the swapped wallet, so messages survive the key switch by design. Finally the operator said push to main; I ran all four gates green and pushed via the dispatch refspec, then was asked to refresh this comms record, which is this write.
narrative.whats_pending:
Grounding correction up front, because the prior narrative was badly out of date: this session did NOT touch the PLAN.md Tier 1 Nostr-substrate items 7 (kind-0 metadata), 8 (kind-1 Share button), or 10 (NIP-05). Those were already shipped by intervening sessions between the prior narrative and now — the git log shows 3e85d0d (item 7 kind-0 profile) and 96de833 (item 8 kind-1 Share to Nostr) landed before this session opened, along with the whole Tier 1 item 11 identity-gate substrate (sub-cuts A through E), full family-unit CRUD, and the key-rotation transport fixes. The prior session.json narrative described the 5/29 session while HEAD had moved roughly thirty commits past it; this overwrite reconciles the comms record to current HEAD (38e8409 on main).

What this session leaves pending: the adopt-existing-key flow is shipped and gated-green but has NOT been field-tested on the operator's device yet. The operator should paste their old Primal nsec into Settings then 'Switch to my existing Nostr key,' confirm the derived old npub, complete the hard-confirm, and verify that holdings survive, that new Nostr posts and profile appear under the old npub, and that existing chat threads keep receiving. The cloud-backup Retry fix wants a field check too — when the banner sticks, tap Retry and confirm it now either clears or tells you to re-sign-in. The update banner will only start firing once a build newer than the installed PWA is loaded once, so the operator may need to force-reload the PWA once to climb onto a build containing the checker.

Known limitations on the adopt flow, surfaced honestly: there is no automatic 'I switched keys' broadcast to peers (the same gap rotation has), so Tapit peers who knew the prior key will not learn of the switch until they re-handshake or walk the succession chain; the operator's old nsec still lives in whatever client they imported it from, so two copies exist; and the switch is forward-only.
narrative.what_you_could_do_better:
Two honest observations. First, I mis-scoped 'cloud not refreshing it's stale' on the first read — I assumed it meant the cockpit's session.json narrative (which was independently stale, so the assumption was not baseless) and built a whole chip-form question around refreshing the comms record before the operator's 'Cloud backup in app' answer redirected me to the actual in-app Supabase banner. The lesson: when the operator says 'cloud' in a field-test context, the in-app surface they are looking at is the more likely referent than the cockpit plumbing, and I should have asked the disambiguating question first instead of leading with my own mis-scope.

Second, the adopt-existing-key feature is genuinely identity-critical and I shipped it in a single session behind gates and a hard-confirm, but it has zero real-device validation yet. The ten unit tests prove the succession assembly and holdings preservation in jsdom, but the full round-trip — encrypt under the operator's real passphrase, persist to Supabase, reload, decrypt, publish under the old npub, receive a chat addressed to the old key — has only been reasoned about, not observed. For something that swaps a wallet's signing identity, the unit-test green is necessary but not sufficient, and the operator's field test is the real gate. Nothing else surfaced beyond declared scope.
narrative.bigger_picture:
The teaching this session is the grounding gate earning its keep twice in one sitting. Two of the operator's four feature-shaped prompts — the update banner and, partially, the cloud-refresh — turned out to be things that already existed or were already correct, and only reading the actual code before building kept me from shipping a duplicate update-checker or 'fixing' a detection chain that was not broken. The version-checker prompt is the cleanest example: the honest answer was not code, it was 'you built this yesterday, here is why it is not visible yet (bootstrap timing), and here is the one real wart worth cleaning (the SW cache leak).' A carpenter who trusted the prompt instead of the repo would have re-implemented a working feature. The discipline of verify-do-not-trust, including not trusting the operator's framing of their own symptom, is what turned four prompts into three small correct commits plus two honest no-code answers.

The deeper thread is what the adopt-existing-key cut means for the Nostr-substrate thesis the prior sessions established. The import-existing-nsec flow (item 9) opened the wallet to existing Nostr users at ONBOARDING — fresh installs could come in as their old identity. This session closed the other half: an operator who ALREADY set up a Tapit wallet, accumulated holdings, built a family ring and a recovery cohort, can now retroactively adopt their established Nostr identity without throwing any of that away. The succession chain is the load-bearing primitive that makes both halves non-destructive — it was built for key rotation, and it turns out 'rotate to a key I supply' is the exact shape of 'become my old identity.'

That is the chassis paying dividends: a primitive built for one purpose (succession after compromise) cleanly serves a purpose nobody designed it for (identity adoption), because the underlying model — identity is the genesis key, the active key is whatever the verifiable chain resolves to — was the right abstraction. The N-to-N growth path the prior session named now works in both temporal directions: bring your identity in when you start, or adopt it after you have already built on Tapit. The substrate flows through the existing Nostr network from either entry point, which is the Mycelium-flow framing the operator set as the thesis for this whole arc.

feedback_to_appcommander: Two patterns worth lifting into the skeleton. First, the grounding gate prevented duplicate work twice this session — the operator asked for a version-update banner and a 'cloud refresh' that already existed or already worked, and only reading the repo before building caught it. The carpenter doctrine already has the grounding gate; what is worth adding is the explicit corollary that the carpenter should not trust the operator's framing of their own symptom in a field-test context — the surface they are looking at and the bug they are inferring are both hypotheses to verify against code. Second, this session is a clean case study of a chassis primitive paying unplanned dividends: createSuccessionLink plus fromSnapshot were built for post-compromise key rotation, and 'rotate to a key I supply' turned out to be the exact shape of 'adopt my old identity into an existing wallet' — zero chassis changes, pure app-layer assembly. The lesson for spawned projects: when a feature request sounds destructive ('replace my identity'), check whether an existing primitive already models the non-destructive version before building a new mechanism or warning the operator off. The right abstraction (identity equals the genesis key, the active key equals the chain-resolved key) made a feature nobody designed for fall out for free.
